summary: Describes the Connectivity Provisioning Profile and a template to capture IP/MPLS connectivity requirements such as reachability and bandwidth, which can help automate service negotiation and activation.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7297 defines a standard form in which one company states the network connection it wants. The form lists where the traffic must reach, how fast it must arrive, how reliable the service must be and how much it may carry. It keeps the customer's requirements separate from the provider's own technology, so the order can be handled by a system rather than by hand.

subtitle: A standard form for stating what an IP connection must do, so a provider can build it without weeks of meetings.

tldr.problem: Orders for IP connectivity are negotiated by email and meeting, and each one starts from scratch, so provisioning a new service takes days or weeks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7297 defines a Connectivity Provisioning Profile, a fixed list of clauses covering reachability, performance guarantees, availability, capacity, isolation, flow identification and activation, written without reference to any one technology.
tldr.outcome: Both sides can exchange the same document instead of writing their own, which lets negotiation and activation be automated and lets traffic engineering and management systems work from the agreed terms.

facts.value: Source Nets, Destination Nets, Guarantees, Scope

today: RFC 7297 is an Informational RFC published in July 2014. The unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a template rather than a protocol, so it can be read alongside whatever technology a provider uses to carry the traffic.

sections.title: The Connectivity Provisioning Interface
sections.content:
The document defines an IP connectivity service as a transfer capability described by four things: the source networks, meaning a group of unicast IP addresses; the destination networks, meaning a group of unicast or multicast addresses; the guarantees, expressed as quality of service, performance and availability; and the scope, meaning the perimeter of the network inside which those guarantees must hold. The scope can sit between the customer's own edge routers and the provider's edge routers.

Between a customer and a network provider there is a Connectivity Provisioning Interface, and the profile is meant to travel across it. The document shows three places that interface can appear: between a customer and a network provider, between a service and a network provider, and between two peer networks. The customer in this picture may be an enterprise buying a VPN service, a service provider buying transit, or another network provider.

The provider sees the connectivity service as a black box, and reports and notifications are sent back to the customer nodes so that the service actually delivered can be compared with what was agreed.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names four things that together describe a connection: where the traffic starts, where it must end, what quality it must have, and over which part of the network the promise holds. The description is written as a document that one side sends to the other across a provisioning interface.

sections.title: Why a Common Order Form Is Needed
sections.content:
Negotiating an IP service takes days or weeks because the customer and the provider sit down and discuss the parameters one at a time, and every new order repeats the whole discussion. The document argues that the two sides have very similar requirements each time, but no standard checklist exists that the customer could fill in.

The requirements a customer typically states are a reachability scope, a direction, a bandwidth requirement, quality of service parameters such as one-way delay, loss or one-way delay variation, protection, and high-availability guidelines such as restoration in less than 50 ms, 100 ms or 1 second. Only afterwards are these turned into technical clauses, and still later into concrete network features: Multiprotocol Label Switching Traffic Engineering, the Resource Reservation Protocol, OSPF or IS-IS.

The document also warns against creating a separate class of service for every profile, because customer-specific rules would multiply the number of classes the network has to engineer and carry. Instead, a small number of generic classes should be defined, and each profile mapped onto one of them. The profile can also be used to size the network, so that routers, cards and link capacity are in place before the traffic arrives. Three benefits are claimed: faster service delivery through automation of negotiation and activation, objectives for traffic engineering and service management functions, and management systems that can make decisions from the agreed profiles.
sections.plainLanguage: Each order used to be argued from scratch, so it took days or weeks even though the questions were similar every time. The profile lists those questions once. It also asks the network to be built around a few generic service classes, so one new customer does not create a new kind of traffic to engineer.

sections.title: Reachability Scope
sections.content:
The scope clause states the reachability of each customer node, seen separately from incoming and outgoing traffic, so it is a unidirectional parameter and both directions are written down. A global scope means the customer site can reach any destination on the Internet and can be reached from any remote host. A restricted scope means no global reachability is allowed: only a named set of destinations may be reached from the site, and only a named set of sources may reach it. Both IPv4 and IPv6 scopes can be given, and the clause may cover multicast as well as unicast addresses, with a group of unicast source addresses added for Source-Specific Multicast.

The clause can also mark the part of the network, topological or geographical, beyond which the performance and availability guarantees stop applying. That part is described by its ingress points and its egress points, which may be customer nodes, provider nodes or external nodes, identified unambiguously by an IPv6 prefix or by a set of IP destinations.

Three models of reachability are described. The 1:1 pipe model allows only point-to-point communications. The 1:N hose model allows communications from one site towards a set of destinations. The 1:any unspecified hose model allows all outbound communications.
sections.plainLanguage: This clause says where the traffic may go and where it may come from. It can be open to the whole internet or closed to named destinations, and it is written one direction at a time, so the return path is listed separately. It can also be limited to one site, to one site sending to many, or to one site sending anywhere.

sections.title: The Clauses of the Profile
sections.content:
A profile begins with a map of the customer nodes to be connected, each identified unambiguously, with the border link or node that connects it and optional geolocation information. The quality of service clause then states the performance metrics a flow must see, such as traffic loss, one-way delay or one-way delay variation, given as a qualitative promise, an average value, a maximum bound or a percentile over an interval, and applying only to in-profile traffic. The availability clause states the percentage of time during which those guarantees hold, as a maximum or an average, covering both a service that is up but below its bounds and a service that is down. Examples of the mechanisms that can meet it are Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, Label Switched Path Ping, pre-installed backup paths, Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol and IP Fast Reroute.

The capacity clause states how much traffic the network must carry, per direction and per border link, and the conformance traffic clause says what happens to traffic above that limit: it may be discarded or moved to a lower class, for example the Lower Effort Per-Domain Behavior. Packet MTU conditions may be stated too. Where neither capacity nor conformance traffic is given, overall traffic guarantees apply, and if those are absent, best effort forwarding is implied.

The remaining clauses cover traffic isolation, which says whether the customer's traffic must be kept apart and can be turned into VPN policy such as IPsec tunnels or BGP/MPLS VPN facilities; flow identification, which lists the fields that pick out the traffic belonging to this service, such as source and destination address, source and destination port, the Type of Service or Differentiated Services Code Point field, or the tail-end tunnel endpoint; routing and forwarding, which can demand dedicated routes for traffic engineering or resilience, or intermediate functions such as a firewall; activation means, which lists the sessions to bring up, such as an IGP instance, a BGP or Multiprotocol BGP session, or Protocol Independent Multicast; invocation means, which is either implicit, with access limited by capacity, or explicit, using RSVP, RSVP-TE, IGMP or MLD with admission control; and notifications, which says how the management platform is told about events that affect the service, over SNMP, Syslog, CPNP signals, NETCONF event notifications or a phone call.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile is a checklist of everything the provider must promise: which sites are connected, how much traffic they may send, how fast it must arrive, how often the service must be up, which traffic must be kept apart from other customers, and how the service is switched on. Each clause can be read on its own, so a reader looking for the speed requirement finds it without reading the rest.

sections.title: The Profile Template
sections.content:
The document gives the profile as a grammar written in Routing Backus-Naur Form, the syntax of RFC 5511. A connectivity provisioning document holds one or more provisioning components, and each component holds one or more profiles. A profile lists the clauses in a fixed order: the customer nodes map, the scope, the quality of service guarantees, availability, capacity, traffic isolation, conformance traffic, flow identification, overall traffic guarantees, routing and forwarding, activation means, invocation means and notifications, followed by any number of optional information elements such as the metrics used for service assurance or an activation schedule.

Two further clauses are shown for administrative details. The customer description holds a name, contact information with an email address, an optional postal address and optional telephone numbers. The provider description holds a name, contact information and optional Autonomous System numbers. The document notes that other clauses, such as contact points, escalation procedures, incident management and billing, may also be part of an agreement, but it does not detail them.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives a grammar for the profile, so two systems read the same fields in the same order. It also leaves room for extra fields, so a provider can add a schedule, service assurance metrics or contact details.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The document does not define an architecture or a protocol, so it says that the means of assuring the identity of a customer and its ability to expose connectivity requirements to a provider still need to be worked out, and the same for the identity of the provider and its ability to expose its capabilities and to capture the customer's requirements.

Profile documents should be protected against illegitimate modification or withdrawal, and authorization means should be in place; the document leaves the choice of those means to each deployment. The provider must protect the privacy-related information held in a profile, and that information must not be revealed to external parties without the consent of the customers. Providers are also asked to enforce policies that make it harder to recognise a customer from the details in a profile.
sections.plainLanguage: A profile holds customer contact details and the locations of its sites, so the document asks for it to be protected against changes, to be kept confidential, and to be made hard to match back to a particular customer. It does not say how to do this, because the right method depends on the deployment.

cells: Only communications from one site towards a set of destinations are allowed.

viz.caption: THE MAIN CLAUSES OF A CONNECTIVITY PROVISIONING PROFILE

items.title: Customer nodes
items.text: Which customer sites are connected, and through which border link.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Which destinations may be reached, and from where.

items.title: Quality of service
items.text: The delay, loss and delay variation a flow may see.

items.title: Availability
items.text: The share of time the guarantees hold.

items.title: Capacity
items.text: How much traffic may be sent, per direction and per link.

items.title: Traffic isolation
items.text: Whether the traffic is kept apart from other customers.

data.title: Connectivity provisioning profile
data.code:
<CONNECTIVITY_PROVISIONING_DOCUMENT> ::=
                       <Connectivity Provisioning Component> ...
<Connectivity Provisioning Component> ::=
                       <CONNECTIVITY_PROVISIONING_PROFILE> ...
<CONNECTIVITY_PROVISIONING_PROFILE> ::=
                       <Customer Nodes Map>
                       <Scope>
                       <QoS Guarantees>
                       <Availability>
                       <Capacity>
                       <Traffic Isolation>
                       <Conformance Traffic>
                       <Flow Identification>
                       <Overall Traffic Guarantees>
                       <Routing and Forwarding>
                       <Activation Means>
                       <Invocation Means>
                       <Notifications>
                       <Optional Information Element> ...
